criteria.note: Ball valves with red handles and water meters are visible in an open floor access hatch.
Two red-and-grey lever handles are clearly visible on the pipes.
No drips, water or stains visible on the valves or pipes; the area is dark but readable.

rows.note: Flat's tiled access hatch: two red-lever ball valves, filters and water meters, no visible leak or stains. Lever position must not be judged.

criteria.note: A blue ball valve body is visible below the water meter, though partly cut off at the bottom edge.
The blue lever handle is visible at the bottom of the frame, partly cropped.
The visible valve and fittings show no drips, water or stains.

rows.note: Outdoor meter with a blue-lever ball valve below; the valve is partly cut off at the bottom edge, so a retake is defensible.

criteria.note: The photo shows the top of a water meter with its display, not a shut-off valve.
No valve handle or lever is visible; only a meter and a blue button.
No valve is in frame, so leaks at a valve cannot be judged.

rows.retakeHint: Step back and photograph the shut-off valve on the pipe, with its handle and the surrounding pipework in frame.
rows.note: Electronic water meter lying on a table, not installed; no shut-off valve in frame.

criteria.note: Several valves are visible on the outdoor water pipework beside the meters.
Small handles are visible on valves, for example at the left pipe and on the vertical riser.
Pipes look weathered, but black-and-white and plants make it hard to judge rust or stains at the valves.

rows.retakeHint: Take a closer colour photo of the one valve that serves your flat, with its handle and the pipe joints clear of plants.
rows.note: Black-and-white outdoor wall with several meters and small valves of a shared building; which valve is the home's is unclear and corrosion can't be judged in B/W. Corroded pipework makes fix_first defensible. Never verified.

criteria.note: The photo shows a water meter dial, not a shut-off valve.
No valve handle or lever is visible; only the meter face and its housing.
No valve is in frame, so leaks at the valve cannot be judged.

rows.retakeHint: Step back and photograph the shut-off valve itself, with its handle or lever, near the meter or pipe.
rows.note: Close-up of a dirty meter dial, no valve in frame (sample photo).

criteria.note: This is an outdoor excavation with a water meter box and pipe fittings, not the flat's own shut-off valve.
No valve handle or lever is clearly visible, only buried pipe fittings and a meter box.
No valve is in view, and the pipe fittings are too small and dirty to judge.

rows.retakeHint: Photograph the shut-off valve inside the flat, such as under the sink or where the main pipe enters, with the handle in view.
rows.note: Street excavation with the utility's meter box, lid closed, no lever visible; wrong subject (the valve is inside the building).

criteria.note: A brass ball valve is visible on a vertical pipe against the wall.
A metal lever with a green grip is visible beside the valve.
No drips, water stains or corrosion visible on the valve or nearby wall; only ordinary solder and patina.

rows.note: Brass ball valve with a green lever on copper pipe, clean (sample photo).

criteria.note: A brass ball valve is visible between copper pipes.
A dark lever handle with a metal bracket hangs below the valve.
No drips, water or stains visible at the valve or soldered joints.

rows.note: Brass ball valve on copper pipe with a black lever; the lever position is ambiguous but never judged.

criteria.note: Only a close-up of a braided hose section is shown; neither the valve end nor the machine end is visible.
No shut-off valve is visible in this close-up of braided hose.
Connections are not visible, and only a short hose section is in focus, so the whole hose can't be judged.

rows.retakeHint: Step back so the whole hose is in frame, from the wall valve to the machine connection, with both ends in focus.
rows.note: Macro of a braided steel hose only: neither the machine nor its tap is in frame.

criteria.note: Only part of a braided hose is shown; the machine end is cut off at the top and it is a close-up.
Only a small part of a valve at the bottom is visible and it is out of focus and cut off.
The visible braided section looks undamaged, but the connections are blurred and partly cut off, so it can't be fully judged.

rows.retakeHint: Step back and take a sharp, well-lit photo showing the whole hose from the wall valve to the machine, with the valve fully in frame.
rows.note: Braided hose into a chrome angle valve, shallow focus; no machine in frame, so the hose is not visible from tap to machine.

criteria.note: A white P-shaped sink trap is clearly visible in frame.
A stream of water is dripping from the bottom of the trap bend.

rows.fix: Clean the drain or trap: lift off the cover, remove hair and dirt, and rinse. If a nut leaks, tighten it.
rows.note: White plastic sink trap with water dripping from it: leak at the trap, urgent (sample photo).

criteria.note: Photo shows a loose brass valve part with thread tape held in hand, not an installed dishwasher connection.
Only a detached brass fitting is shown, not an installed dishwasher shut-off valve.
No installed hose or connection is visible, so leaks cannot be judged.

rows.retakeHint: Photograph the installed dishwasher hose and shut-off valve under the sink, with the whole connection in frame.
rows.note: A hand holding a loose brass valve with thread tape: a loose part, not an installed connection. Never describe the person.

criteria.note: Under-sink white plastic waste pipe with a bottle-style trap and compression nuts is visible.
No drips, standing water or stains on the trap, joints or cabinet floor.

rows.note: Open under-sink cupboard: plastic trap with an appliance branch, dry clean floor, no leak. (No drip tray, but that is L4, not L5.)

criteria.note: Under-sink cabinet is open but a person's legs block the view; no trap is clearly visible.
The trap and drain area is hidden, so leaks or blockage can't be judged.

rows.retakeHint: Take a close photo of the pipe under the sink with nothing blocking the view and good light.
rows.note: A person lying in an open sink cupboard (legs only); the trap is not clearly visible. Never describe the person.

criteria.note: Only the sink strainer openings are visible; the trap is hidden behind closed cabinet doors and no floor drain is shown.
The sink strainers show no standing water, but the trap and pipes below can't be seen.

rows.retakeHint: Open the cupboard under the sink and photograph the pipes and trap clearly with good light.
rows.note: Kitchen with the lower cupboard doors closed; the trap is not visible (sample photo).

criteria.note: The braided hose connects to a toilet cistern or basin, not a dishwasher.
An angle valve is visible, but it serves a toilet or basin, so it cannot be tied to a dishwasher.
No drips, water stains, kinks or bulges are visible on the hose, valve or fittings.

rows.retakeHint: Retake showing the dishwasher's own water hose and shut-off valve, usually under the sink next to the dishwasher.
rows.note: Toilet supply: braided hose and angle stop valve under a toilet cistern; wrong appliance for the dishwasher check.

criteria.note: A distribution board with rows of ABB breakers and blank cover panels fills the frame.
Covers and blanking plates are in place, with no scorch marks, damage or exposed live parts visible.
Several RCDs with round TEST buttons and blue levers are visible, including an ABB F204 on the lower right.
Nothing is stored in front of or against the board.

rows.note: Modern ABB board: RCDs with TEST buttons, B16 breakers, labelled circuits, cover on (sample photo).

criteria.note: An old electricity meter board with fuse holders is visible in a wall recess.
Fuse covers and caps are removed and lying loose; wiring and terminals appear exposed, with dark soot-like staining.
No RCD with a TEST button is visible on this board.
Tools, removed fuse covers and parts are lying in front of the board.

rows.fix: Clear the space in front of the fuse box. If you see damage or scorch marks, or there is no RCD, call an authorised electrician. Do not fix it yourself.
rows.note: Old single-phase installation with porcelain screw-fuse holders, a removed fuse and tools on the floor: exposed parts, no RCD.

criteria.note: An empty distribution board enclosure and its separate cover are shown, with no devices installed.
The enclosure is empty and the cover is detached, so this looks like an uninstalled product rather than a fitted board.
No RCD or other devices are installed; only an empty DIN rail and terminal bars are visible.
Nothing is stored in front, but the unit is not installed and the cover has packaging film on it.

rows.retakeHint: Photograph the installed, fitted fuse box with its cover on and the RCD with its TEST button in view.
rows.note: An empty consumer-unit enclosure with its cover beside it, bare DIN rail, no breakers: not an installed board. fix_first (missing cover, no RCD) is defensible. Never verified.

criteria.note: The whole distribution board is in frame and fills most of the photo.
The cover is off, so terminals, wiring and live connections are exposed.
Three RCBO units are labelled RCBO1, RCBO2 and RC, each with a round test button.
Nothing is stored in front of or against the board.

rows.fix: Clear the space in front of the fuse box. If you see damage or scorch marks, or there is no RCD, call an authorised electrician. Do not fix it yourself.
rows.note: Consumer unit with its front cover removed: RCBOs and exposed terminals, urgent (sample photo).

criteria.note: A wall-mounted breaker panel with its door open is fully in frame.
The cover is in place over the wiring; no scorch marks, damage or exposed live parts are visible.
Two breakers, at positions 6 and 12, have yellow TEST buttons, which look like GFCI/AFCI-type devices.
Nothing is stored in front of or against the panel.

rows.note: US breaker panel, door open, dead front on, handwritten circuit numbers, two GFCI breakers with TEST buttons (residual-current protection).

criteria.note: Only a single isolated RCD device is shown, not a whole fuse box or distribution board.
The device looks intact, but the board and its cover are not shown, so this can't be judged.
An ABB RCD with a TEST button and TEST label is clearly visible.
Isolated device on a plain background, so the area in front of a board can't be judged.

rows.retakeHint: Take a photo of the whole fuse box in your home, with the cover open and the RCD in view, from about one metre away.
rows.note: Product photo of an ABB RCD on a white background: not the home's board.

criteria.note: An old industrial distribution board with many enclosed switch and fuse boxes is fully in frame.
Heavy rust, peeling paint and worn enclosures are visible, and a loose cable loop hangs over one box.
No RCD with a TEST button is visible; only old-style switches and enclosed boxes.
A coiled cable with a plug hangs across the front of one box.

rows.fix: Clear the space in front of the fuse box. If you see damage or scorch marks, or there is no RCD, call an authorised electrician. Do not fix it yourself.
rows.note: Old industrial cast-metal switchgear (ASEA) with covers on but no RCD visible. A retake (not a home board) is defensible. Never verified.

criteria.note: A wall-mounted distribution board with its door open is clearly in frame.
Door is open and fuse holders, terminals and wiring are exposed, with loose cables and a blue part on top.
Fuses, a meter and a small breaker are visible, but no RCD with a TEST button can be seen.
Nothing is stored in front of or against the board.

rows.fix: Clear the space in front of the fuse box. If you see damage or scorch marks, or there is no RCD, call an authorised electrician. Do not fix it yourself.
rows.note: Open metal cabinet in an outbuilding: meter, screw fuses, main switch and exposed empty fuse bases; RCD not clearly visible.
